summary: Describes how to test and measure the performance of devices that forward IP multicast traffic. It builds on earlier benchmarking methodology work such as RFC 2544 and extends it from one-to-one traffic to one-to-many traffic. It is a methodology guide for testers, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A teacher reads one story to a whole class at once. This memo explains how to time and score how well a network box can do that kind of one-to-many delivery.

questions: how do igmp group changes affect device performance
how is latency measured in multicast routing
subtitle: Testing and measuring how well devices forward one-to-many traffic.

tldr.problem: Network equipment needs to be tested for multicast forwarding performance, but benchmarking methodologies for multicast are limited. Existing benchmarking work assumes one-to-one traffic patterns.
tldr.mechanism: This document extends RFC 2544 benchmarking methodology from unicast to multicast, defining tests for throughput, latency, overhead and capacity of multicast forwarding devices.
tldr.outcome: Testers and vendors now have a standardized set of methodologies to measure and report multicast device performance fairly and consistently.

facts.label: Max egress interfaces per test
facts.value: Limited only by test apparatus and DUT capacity

today: RFC 3918 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It remains the standard methodology for multicast device benchmarking and is used by vendors and network testers to document device performance.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.content:
RFC 3918 defines testing methodologies specific to IP multicast forwarding devices – network equipment that takes one incoming stream and duplicates it to many outgoing ports simultaneously. The document builds on earlier benchmarking work in RFC 2544 and RFC 2432 (multicast terminology) to extend those methods to the one-to-many traffic case.

The key challenge is that multicast devices behave differently from unicast routers. Instead of finding the single path to a destination, multicast routers build multicast forwarding databases listing which egress ports should receive which multicast groups. Testing must account for group membership changes, variable numbers of groups, and the overhead of joining and leaving multicast groups.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular network tests measure sending a package to one person. Multicast tests measure sending the same package to a group of people at once, which requires different ways to measure success.

sections.title: Multicast Testing Fundamentals
sections.content:
All tests in the document follow a common topology with one source test port and multiple destination test ports. The Device Under Test (DUT) sits in the middle, receiving multicast traffic on an ingress port and forwarding it to egress ports based on Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) group membership reports sent by destination ports.

Critical test setup considerations include IGMP version consistency, standard frame sizes (64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1280, and 1518 bytes for Ethernet), Time-To-Live (TTL) values that let traffic traverse the device, and test duration of at least 30 seconds. The test apparatus must validate correct forwarding before and after each measurement.
sections.plainLanguage: To fairly test a device, you need one sender, many receivers, and clear rules about frame sizes and how long the test runs. You also need to verify the test worked correctly.

sections.title: Key Performance Metrics
sections.content:
The RFC defines six major categories of measurements:

Forwarding throughput tests measure the maximum load a device can forward without dropping frames. Mixed class throughput tests unicast and multicast traffic together, scaled group forwarding tests vary the number of active multicast groups, and aggregated multicast throughput tests the maximum sustainable rate across all egress ports.

Tunneling throughput tests encapsulation (wrapping multicast packets for transmission), decapsulation (unwrapping them), and re-encapsulation (converting between tunnel formats).

Forwarding latency measures the time from when a packet enters the device to when it exits each egress port. Min/max multicast latency reports the difference between the fastest and slowest exit times.

Overhead delays measure how long group join and leave operations take – critical because routers must start and stop forwarding quickly when users join or leave multicast sessions.

Multicast group capacity determines how many groups a device can simultaneously support.
sections.plainLanguage: Tests measure how much traffic can flow, how fast packets cross the device, how quickly groups can be added or removed, and how many groups fit at once.

sections.title: Realistic and Interaction Testing
sections.content:
Beyond basic metrics, the RFC includes tests for real-world conditions. Forwarding burdened multicast latency measures latency while the device simultaneously handles unicast traffic – simulating a device carrying both types of traffic. Similarly, forwarding burdened group join delay tests group membership changes under unicast load.

These interaction tests reveal how device architecture affects performance when multiple traffic types compete for resources. Some devices dedicate separate data paths for multicast and unicast; others process both through a shared pipeline. Testing under load shows these design differences.
sections.plainLanguage: Real networks make devices do many things at once. These tests see how fast a device can handle multicast when it is also busy with regular one-to-one traffic.

sections.title: Test Procedures and Reporting
sections.content:
Each test type specifies an objective, detailed procedure, and required reporting format. Procedures typically use a binary search algorithm to find the maximum load with zero frame loss or the minimum delay encountered. Test parameters such as frame size, number of egress ports, IGMP version, number of groups, and offered load MUST be disclosed with results.

Results SHOULD be reported in tables showing the relationship between test parameters and outcomes. For example, throughput results show one row per tested frame size, with columns for offered load, frames transmitted, frames received, and measured throughput.

The RFC emphasizes that test results are specific to the tested topology and configuration. Modifications to accommodation of different transmission media MUST be documented. A trial is INVALID if unexpected differences occur between intended and actual load, frames are improperly formed, required frames are not forwarded on all expected ports, or frames arrive more than 5 seconds after the test ends.
sections.plainLanguage: Each test follows a recipe: try a load, check results, adjust and repeat until you find the limit. Then write down everything you did and what happened.
